subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A medical student is learning cardiac auscultation. Her attending explains the mnemonic for where to listen (APTM) and places the stethoscope at the patient's right second intercostal space at the sternal border. At this location she hears a harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur that radiates to the carotids.
question: Which auscultation area is the stethoscope placed in, and which murmur is classically heard there?

options.text: Pulmonic area (left second intercostal space); pulmonic stenosis and flow murmurs
Tricuspid area (left lower sternal border); tricuspid regurgitation and ventricular septal defect
Aortic area (right second intercostal space); aortic stenosis
Mitral area (apex, fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line); mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis
Left sternal border; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic regurgitation

explanation_correct: The auscultation areas follow the mnemonic APTM: Aortic (right second intercostal space), Pulmonic (left second intercostal space), Tricuspid (left lower sternal border), Mitral (apex, fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line). The aortic area is where the crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur of aortic stenosis is loudest and from which it radiates to the carotids.

explanation_incorrect.A: The pulmonic area lies at the left, not the right, second intercostal space; it is where pulmonic stenosis, atrial septal defect, and flow murmurs are heard.
explanation_incorrect.B: The tricuspid area is at the left lower sternal border and is the site of tricuspid regurgitation and ventricular septal defect murmurs, not the right second intercostal space.
explanation_incorrect.D: The mitral area is at the apex in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, far from the right second intercostal space; it is where mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, and mitral stenosis are heard.
explanation_incorrect.E: The left sternal border is where hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic and pulmonic regurgitation murmurs are best heard; it is not the right second intercostal space.

educationalObjective: The auscultation areas (APTM) are Aortic at the right 2nd intercostal space, Pulmonic at the left 2nd ICS, Tricuspid at the left lower sternal border, and Mitral at the apex.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man is being evaluated for a diastolic murmur heard at the left sternal border. The examiner asks him to perform sustained isometric hand grip. During the maneuver, the murmur becomes louder; another systolic murmur noted at the same visit becomes softer during the grip.
question: Which of the following best explains the effect of sustained hand grip on these two murmurs?

options.text: Hand grip decreases afterload, which increases forward flow across stenotic valves and decreases regurgitant flow

Hand grip markedly increases afterload, increasing the reverse flow across the aortic valve, so regurgitant murmurs such as aortic regurgitation intensify while the transvalvular gradient in aortic stenosis falls and its murmur softens
Hand grip decreases preload, shrinking the ventricular cavity and thereby increasing flow through any narrowed valve
Hand grip increases venous return to the right heart, selectively amplifying right-sided murmurs and silencing left-sided ones
Hand grip increases preload, enlarging the ventricular cavity and worsening dynamic outflow obstruction, so most left-sided murmurs soften

explanation_correct: Sustained hand grip produces a strong increase in afterload, which increases reverse flow across the aortic valve. Regurgitant and shunt lesions—most other left-sided murmurs such as aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, and ventricular septal defect—therefore intensify. Aortic stenosis softens because the raised aortic pressure decreases the transaortic valve pressure gradient, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy softens because increased left ventricular volume lessens the dynamic obstruction.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hand grip increases, not decreases, afterload; decreased afterload would not explain the louder regurgitant murmur, and increased forward flow across a stenotic valve is not what happens during grip.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hand grip does not decrease preload; the murmur that softened (aortic stenosis) did so because its pressure gradient fell with higher aortic pressure, not because of a shrunken cavity.
explanation_incorrect.D: Increased venous return to the right heart with inspiration, not hand grip, selectively amplifies right-sided murmurs; hand grip primarily raises afterload and affects left-sided lesions.
explanation_incorrect.E: An increase in preload with an enlarged cavity reducing dynamic obstruction explains why hypertrophic cardiomyopathy softens, but hand grip works chiefly through afterload, and most other left-sided murmurs (AR, MR, VSD) increase during grip.

educationalObjective: Sustained hand grip markedly increases afterload, intensifying AR/MR/VSD murmurs while softening aortic stenosis (decreased transaortic gradient) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 26-year-old woman has a late crescendo murmur at the apex preceded by a click. When she stands up or performs the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver, the click occurs earlier in systole, closer to the first heart sound, and the murmur lengthens.
question: Which of the following best explains the change in this patient's murmur during these maneuvers?

options.text: Decreased preload increases flow through the stenotic mitral valve, delaying valve closure and the accompanying click
Increased afterload raises the transvalvular gradient and pushes the click and murmur later in systole
Increased venous return enlarges the left ventricle, delaying the onset of leaflet prolapse until late systole
Maneuvers that decrease venous return delay pulmonic valve closure, moving the click closer to the second heart sound
A smaller left ventricular volume allows the mitral leaflets to prolapse earlier in systole, producing an earlier midsystolic click and an earlier-onset murmur

explanation_correct: This patient has mitral valve prolapse, with a midsystolic click followed by a late crescendo murmur at the apex. Standing and the strain phase of Valsalva both decrease preload (decrease left ventricular volume). With a smaller ventricular cavity, the mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium earlier in systole, so the midsystolic click—produced by sudden tensing of the chordae tendineae—occurs earlier and the murmur begins sooner.

explanation_incorrect.A: Standing and Valsalva do not increase flow through a stenotic valve; there is no mitral stenosis here, and the click moves earlier, not later, because prolapse begins sooner.
explanation_incorrect.B: These maneuvers decrease preload rather than increase afterload; the click and murmur move earlier in systole, not later.
explanation_incorrect.C: Venous return and ventricular size decrease during standing and Valsalva strain; an enlarged ventricle delaying prolapse is the mechanism of passive leg raise, which has the opposite effect (later click).
explanation_incorrect.D: The timing change involves the mitral apparatus, not pulmonic valve closure; the click in MVP comes from chordae tendineae tensing as leaflets prolapse.

educationalObjective: Standing and Valsalva decrease preload and LV volume, causing an earlier midsystolic click in mitral valve prolapse; most other murmurs decrease with these maneuvers.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 40-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use has a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. The murmur clearly becomes louder when she inhales deeply and softer when she exhales. A second murmur heard at the apex does not increase with inspiration but becomes more prominent during expiration.
question: Which of the following best explains the differing effect of respiration on these two murmurs?

options.text: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, amplifying right-sided murmurs such as tricuspid regurgitation, while left-sided murmurs such as mitral regurgitation increase with expiration
Inspiration increases venous return to the left heart, so left-sided murmurs such as mitral regurgitation grow louder on inspiration
Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure, which decreases flow across all four valves and softens every murmur
Expiration increases venous return to the right heart, which explains why the left lower sternal border murmur was louder during expiration
Inspiration raises afterload, increasing reverse flow across the tricuspid valve, while leaving mitral flow unchanged

explanation_correct: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so most right-sided murmurs—such as tricuspid regurgitation, which this patient likely has from endocarditis or right ventricular dilatation—increase with inspiration. Simultaneously, inspiration decreases venous return to the left heart, so most left-sided murmurs, such as the apical mitral regurgitation murmur, increase with expiration instead. This respiratory behavior is a standard bedside tool for localizing a murmur to the right or left side of the heart.

explanation_incorrect.B: Inspiration decreases, not increases, venous return to the left heart; the apical murmur grew louder during expiration, consistent with left-sided physiology.
explanation_incorrect.C: Inspiration increases right-sided flow rather than uniformly decreasing flow across all valves; the right lower sternal border murmur became louder, not softer, on inspiration.
explanation_incorrect.D: Inspiration, not expiration, increases venous return to the right heart; the inspiration-louder murmur at the left lower sternal border is right-sided.
explanation_incorrect.E: Afterload changes do not drive the respiratory variation; the mechanism is altered venous return, and mitral flow is not unchanged—it is reduced during inspiration.

educationalObjective: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart (right-sided murmurs louder) and decreases return to the left heart (left-sided murmurs louder with expiration).

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 21-year-old man with a systolic murmur at the left sternal border is examined during several maneuvers. When he squats, his murmur becomes noticeably softer; when he stands rapidly from squatting, the murmur becomes louder and the pulse contour shows a brisk upstroke followed by obstruction. The murmur is also louder during the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver.
question: Which of the following best explains the effect of squatting on this patient's murmur?

options.text: Squatting decreases preload, shrinking the ventricular cavity and intensifying outflow obstruction
Squatting decreases afterload, increasing reverse flow across the aortic valve and thereby softening regurgitant murmurs
Squatting raises the transaortic valve pressure gradient, increasing flow through the narrowed valve and amplifying the ejection murmur
Squatting increases both preload and afterload, increasing left ventricular volume, which reduces the dynamic outflow obstruction and softens the murmur
Squatting decreases venous return to the right heart while increasing it to the left heart, selectively softening left-sided murmurs

explanation_correct: This patient has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, whose systolic murmur at the left sternal border intensifies with maneuvers that decrease left ventricular volume (standing, Valsalva strain) and softens with maneuvers that increase left ventricular volume. Squatting increases both preload and afterload, which increases left ventricular volume; the larger, fuller ventricle lessens the dynamic outflow tract obstruction, so the murmur softens—opposite to what happens when he stands. Hand grip also softens this murmur for the same reason.

explanation_incorrect.A: Squatting increases, not decreases, preload; a shrunken ventricular cavity with more obstruction describes standing or Valsalva strain, the maneuvers that made this murmur louder.
explanation_incorrect.B: Squatting increases afterload rather than decreasing it, and the murmur here is the dynamic obstruction of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not a regurgitant lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Raising the transaortic gradient describes aortic stenosis, whose murmur actually decreases with squatting; this patient's murmur pattern (louder standing and with Valsalva) points to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Squatting does not differentially redistribute venous return between the two sides of the heart; its effect is a simultaneous increase in preload and afterload.

educationalObjective: Squatting increases preload and afterload, increasing LV volume and softening the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur while intensifying most other murmurs.
